lessons.title: After-Tax Returns: How Rent and Capital Gains Are Taxed Differently

children.text: Every return in this course so far has been calculated before tax. That is useful for comparing properties, but you cannot spend a pre-tax return. And for property, tax does not treat the two engines equally. Rent is taxed every single year at your income tax slab rate. Appreciation is taxed only once, when you sell, at a flat rate that for most long-term owners is far lower. That difference can quietly reverse which property looks better. By the end of this lesson you will be able to calculate the tax on rental income, estimate capital gains tax on a sale, see how tax changes the gap between a high-yield office and a growth-driven flat, and know the main legal ways to reduce the bill.

body.text: Rent is taxed every year at your slab rate. Appreciation is taxed once, at sale, at a lower flat rate. Two properties with the same pre-tax return can leave you with very different after-tax returns, and tax usually narrows the lead of high-yield property.

Tax rules change. The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaced the Income-tax Act, 1961 from 1 April 2026 and renumbered its sections, so older references such as "Section 24" or "Section 54" now have new numbers. This lesson describes the rules as they apply to resident individuals at the time of writing, using the old section names only where they are still widely used. Always confirm current rules with a chartered accountant before filing or selling.

children.text: How Rental Income Is Taxed

markDefs.definition: The income tax category for rent earned from buildings, including flats, offices and shops that you own and let out.
A flat 30% deduction from rental income, after municipal taxes, allowed in place of actual repairs, maintenance and other running costs.

children.text: Rent from a flat, office or shop you let out is taxed as
income from house property
. The calculation has three steps: start with rent received, subtract municipal property tax you actually paid, then take a
30% standard deduction
. Interest on a loan taken to buy the let-out property can also be deducted, which we cover below. What remains is added to your other income and taxed at your slab rate.

body.latex: \text{Taxable Rental Income} = (\text{Rent Received} - \text{Municipal Taxes Paid}) \times 70\% - \text{Home Loan Interest}
body.caption: The 30% standard deduction is applied after municipal taxes and before loan interest.
Tax on a year's rent from a ₹1 crore flat, owner in the 30% slab (illustrative, no loan)

cells: Pre-tax net operating income (after ₹50,000 of other running costs)

children.text: The flat's net yield falls from 2.4% before tax to about 1.77% after tax. Tax takes roughly a quarter of the net rent, every year, for as long as the flat is let.

body.text: The 30% standard deduction replaces your actual running costs. Society maintenance, repairs, repainting, brokerage and insurance are not deducted separately, however much you spend. If your real costs are well below 30% of rent, the deduction works in your favour; if they are higher, it does not.

body.title: Tax on rent
body.prompt: A shop in Indore earns rent of ₹4,80,000 a year. The owner pays ₹12,000 in municipal property tax and has no loan. The owner's slab rate is 20%, plus 4% cess (20.8% in total). How much income tax is due on the rent, in rupees? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: Net annual value = ₹4,80,000 − ₹12,000 = ₹4,68,000. Less 30% standard deduction of ₹1,40,400 = taxable rent of ₹3,27,600. Tax = ₹3,27,600 × 20.8% = ₹68,140.80, or about ₹68,141.

children.text: How Capital Gains on Property Are Taxed

markDefs.definition: The period between buying and selling an asset. For land and buildings, more than 24 months makes a gain long-term.
Purchase price plus costs of buying it, such as stamp duty and registration, which is subtracted from the sale price to find the gain.

children.text: When you sell, the gain is the sale price minus selling costs such as brokerage, minus your
cost of acquisition
and any cost of improvement. How it is taxed depends on the
holding period

body.caption: Capital gains on land and buildings for resident individuals

body.latex: \text{LTCG} = \text{Sale Price} - \text{Selling Costs} - (\text{Purchase Price} + \text{Stamp Duty and Registration} + \text{Improvements})
body.caption: Tax = LTCG × 12.5%, plus 4% cess, giving an effective 13% before any surcharge.

children.text: Continue with the ₹1 crore flat, bought with ₹7 lakh of stamp duty and registration and sold after ten years at 6% annual growth. It sells for about ₹1.79 crore. After 1% brokerage, the gain over the ₹1.07 crore cost is about ₹70.3 lakh, and tax at 13% is about ₹9.14 lakh. Over those ten years, the owner also paid about ₹7.97 lakh in tax on rent, even though the rent was far smaller than the appreciation.

body.title: Short or long?
body.question: Kavita buys a flat in Chennai in March 2025 and sells it in November 2026 at a profit. Kavita earns a salary in the 30% slab. How is the profit taxed?
options: At 12.5% as a long-term capital gain
At the 30% slab rate as a short-term capital gain, because it was held for 24 months or less
It is tax-free because it is a residence
body.explanation: March 2025 to November 2026 is about 20 months, within the 24-month limit for land and buildings. The gain is short-term and added to Kavita's income at the slab rate, 30% plus cess. Waiting just a few more months would have made it long-term, taxed at 12.5% plus cess.

body.title: Property bought before 23 July 2024: the indexation choice

markDefs.definition: Adjusting the purchase cost upward for inflation using the Cost Inflation Index, which reduces the taxable gain.

children.text: From 23 July 2024, the long-term capital gains rate on property became 12.5% without
indexation

, replacing the earlier 20% with indexation. For resident individuals and HUFs selling land or buildings bought before that date, the law allows the tax to be calculated both ways, paying whichever is lower.

content.caption: Flat bought in 2015-16 for ₹50 lakh, sold in 2025-26 for ₹1 crore (costs ignored)

cells: Indexed cost = ₹50 lakh × 376 ÷ 254 = ₹74.02 lakh; 20% × (₹1 crore − ₹74.02 lakh)

children.text: Here the indexation route saves about ₹1 lakh, because the flat's price grew only modestly faster than the Cost Inflation Index (254 for 2015-16 and 376 for 2025-26). For properties that appreciated much faster than inflation, the 12.5% route usually wins. Run both calculations every time.
Why Tax Favours Appreciation Over Rent

markDefs.definition: The reduction in annual return caused by taxes, measured as the difference between pre-tax and after-tax XIRR.

children.text: Three things make appreciation tax-efficient: a lower rate (13% versus up to 31.2% on rent), deferral (nothing is paid until you sell, so the untaxed gain keeps compounding), and control (you choose the year of sale and can use reinvestment exemptions). Now compare the flat with a ₹1 crore office unit earning much more rent but growing more slowly. Both carry ₹7 lakh of buying costs, are held ten years, and belong to an owner in the 30% slab. The difference between pre-tax and after-tax XIRR is the
tax drag

body.caption: Ten years on ₹1 crore: flat vs office, before and after tax (illustrative, 30% slab, no loan)

body.title: Ten-Year XIRR Before and After Tax (%)

stats.label: Office's tax drag
stats.context: Mostly paid every year on rent

children.text: Tax cuts the office's lead by more than half. The office still wins in this illustration, but for an owner in a lower slab, the gap would stay wider, and for an owner whose rent pushes them into a higher slab or surcharge, it could close entirely. This is why the same property can be right for one investor and wrong for another.

body.title: Tax on rent vs tax on appreciation

columns.label: Rent
points: Taxed every year it is received
At your slab rate, up to 30% plus cess and surcharge
30% standard deduction instead of actual costs
Hurts high-yield property and high-income owners most

columns.label: Appreciation
points: Taxed only in the year you sell
12.5% plus cess if held more than 24 months
Purchase costs, improvements and selling costs reduce the gain
Reinvestment exemptions can reduce or remove the tax

children.text: Home Loans and Tax

For a let-out property, interest on a loan taken to buy it can be deducted from rental income. With a large loan, interest often exceeds taxable rent, creating a loss from house property. What happens to that loss depends heavily on which tax regime you choose.

body.caption: Let-out ₹1 crore flat with a ₹75 lakh loan: taxable rent ₹2.03 lakh, first-year interest about ₹6.3 lakh

cells: Set off against salary this year
Nil, beyond wiping out tax on the rent
Carried forward up to 8 years, against house property income only

body.text: Interest deductions soften leverage, but they do not rescue a bad deal. In the old regime, ₹62,400 of tax saved barely dents the ₹5.3 lakh first-year cash gap from the last lesson. Treat tax savings as a small bonus, never as the reason to borrow.

children.text: Legal Ways to Reduce Capital Gains Tax
Hold for more than 24 months.
The simplest saving: it moves the gain from your slab rate to 12.5%.
Keep every receipt.
Stamp duty, registration, brokerage on sale and documented improvements such as a new floor or extension all reduce the taxable gain.
Reinvest in a residential house.

Long-term gains from selling a house can be exempt if reinvested in a residential house in India within the prescribed window (commonly known as the Section 54 exemption), subject to limits and a lock-in on the new house.
Invest in specified bonds.

Long-term gains on land or buildings invested within six months in specified bonds such as those issued by NHAI, REC, PFC or IRFC (commonly known as Section 54EC bonds) can be exempt, up to ₹50 lakh, with a five-year lock-in.
Park unused gains correctly.

If you plan to buy or build a house but have not done so by the tax return due date, the gain must be deposited in the Capital Gains Account Scheme at an authorised bank to keep the exemption available.

body.text: Under-reporting the sale price, taking part of it in cash or registering below the stamp duty value is not tax planning. It is illegal, can trigger tax on the stamp duty value anyway, and leaves the buyer and seller exposed to penalties. Use only exemptions and deductions the law actually provides.

body.title: The magic number
body.textWithBlank: A gain on land or a building is long-term if the property was held for more than ___ months.
body.explanation: More than 24 months makes the gain long-term, taxed at 12.5% plus cess. At 24 months or less, it is short-term and taxed at your slab rate.

body.title: What to do with a ₹40 lakh gain
body.scenario: Anjali Singh, a 45-year-old doctor in Lucknow in the 30% slab, sells a flat bought in 2021 for a long-term capital gain of ₹40 lakh after accounting for purchase costs and brokerage. Anjali has no immediate plan to buy another home but might buy one in a year or two. A friend suggests "just put it in an FD".
body.prompt: Estimate the tax if nothing is done, then compare the main options for reducing it and the trade-offs of each.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Tax if nothing is done: ₹40 lakh × 12.5% = ₹5 lakh, plus 4% cess = about ₹5.2 lakh. Because the flat was bought before 23 July 2024, Anjali should also check whether 20% with indexation would be lower, and pay the lower of the two.
2. Specified bonds: investing the full ₹40 lakh gain within six months of sale in eligible bonds, such as those of NHAI, REC, PFC or IRFC, could save about ₹5.2 lakh. The trade-off: five years of lock-in, a fixed interest rate, and interest that is itself taxable at 30%.
3. Residential house exemption: if Anjali buys a residential house within the prescribed period, the gain can be exempt up to the amount reinvested. Since the purchase may take a year or two, the unused gain must be deposited in the Capital Gains Account Scheme before the tax return due date, or the exemption is lost.
4. The FD idea: an FD gives no exemption. Anjali would pay about ₹5.2 lakh now and then tax on the FD interest every year.
5. A mixed approach is possible: bonds for part of the gain and a house purchase for the rest.
6. The deciding question is not just tax saved but what Anjali wants the money to do. Locking ₹40 lakh into bonds for five years or into another property only makes sense if that fits Anjali's plans. A chartered accountant should confirm timelines and eligibility under the current Act.

body.title: Build an after-tax view of any property
steps: Confirm your likely slab rate, including cess and any surcharge, and which tax regime you use.
Calculate yearly tax on rent: (rent − municipal taxes) × 70%, minus eligible loan interest, times your slab rate.
Estimate capital gains at your planned sale date, including purchase costs, improvements and selling brokerage.
Check whether the holding period will exceed 24 months.
For property bought before 23 July 2024, compare 12.5% without indexation and 20% with indexation.
Put after-tax rent and after-tax sale proceeds into your XIRR calculation.
Plan reinvestment exemptions before the sale, not after, and confirm details with a chartered accountant.

cards.definition: The tax category for rent from buildings you own and let out.
A flat deduction from rent after municipal taxes, in place of actual running costs.
A gain on land or buildings held more than 24 months, taxed at 12.5% plus cess.
Raising the purchase cost for inflation using the Cost Inflation Index; optional at 20% for resident individuals on property bought before 23 July 2024.
The fall in XIRR caused by tax, the gap between pre-tax and after-tax return.
Exemption for long-term gains on land or buildings invested in eligible bonds within six months, up to ₹50 lakh, with a five-year lock-in.
A bank deposit scheme for holding gains meant for a house purchase not yet completed by the tax return due date.

points: Rent is taxed every year at your slab rate after municipal taxes and a 30% standard deduction; actual running costs are not deducted separately.
Long-term gains on property held more than 24 months are taxed at 12.5% plus cess, only in the year of sale.
For property bought before 23 July 2024, resident individuals can compare 20% with indexation and pay the lower tax.
Lower rates, deferral and control make appreciation more tax-efficient than rent.
In the illustration, tax cut an office's pre-tax lead over a flat from 1.18 to 0.48 percentage points.
Loan interest on let-out property is deductible, but loss set-off rules differ sharply between the old and new tax regimes.
Use legal tools: hold beyond 24 months, keep receipts, and plan residential house or specified bond exemptions before you sell.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax, legal or investment advice. The people, properties, rents and returns shown are illustrative, and tax figures ignore surcharge and assume resident individual taxpayers. Tax rates, exemptions, section numbers and regime rules change, and the Income-tax Act, 2025 has renumbered many provisions, so consult a chartered accountant before filing, selling or reinvesting.
